div.p: Many complex real-time systems, such as increasingly automated vehicles and 5G wireless base stations, contain a large amount of shared resources that must be accessed in a mutually exclusive fashion. This leads to significant contention especially when resources are shared across processors. To reduce the contention, various resource-aware task allocation methods have been developed to localize the shared resources. Unfortunately, these existing methods either are tailored for specific scheduling and analysis approaches, or introduce runtime overhead that undermines their applicability. In this paper, we present a task allocation method for a mainstream type of real-time systems in practice: FP-FPS (fully-partitioned fixed-priority scheduling) multiprocessor systems with spin locks managing shared resources. Instead of relying on timing bounds as guidance, we utilize a model to approximate the degree of resource contention between tasks. The model is decoupled from priority assignment algorithms, resource sharing protocols and schedulability tests. Hence, our task allocation method can be applied without detailed knowledge of the underlying system, which is particularly useful during the initial design phase of the system. More detailed information about the system in the later phases of design will push up the approximation accuracy and further enhance the performance. Experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms the state-of-the-art by 13.6% on average (up to 24.2%) in system schedulability with a much less (57x on average) computation cost and negligible runtime overhead.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: With ever-complex functionalities being implemented in real-time systems, e.g., autonomous vehicles and base stations for 5G telecommunication, tasks in the system are often required to operate on the same object that must be accessed in a mutually exclusive fashion, including code segments, memory blocks, I/O ports, etc. The spin locks mandated by the AUTOSAR standard [1] are widely adopted for protecting computations on shared resources from race conditions, with a resource sharing protocol applied to manage accesses to shared resources [2]. However, with spin locks enforced, tasks in the system can incur resource contention due to the competition for shared resources. Especially, when tasks request the same resource from different processors, they busy-wait (spin) on their host processors until the requested resource is granted. This leads to a high blocking for potentially all tasks in these processors and can significantly undermine the schedulability of the system [3].

To mitigate resource contention across processors, the resourceaware task allocation has received much attention under the fullypartitioned (FP) multiprocessor systems, which reduces contention by localizing the shared resources. Numerous resource-aware task allocation methods are available for various scheduling methods and resource sharing protocols, e.g., the Fixed-Priority scheduling (FPS) and the Multiprocessor Stack Resource Protocol (MSRP) [4]. These methods can be generally categorized into two major approaches, which execute critical sections (i) on the host processor of tasks or (ii) on dedicated processors. The first approach aims to allocate tasks with the same shared resources to one processor to reduce contention. However, for complex systems with intensive resource sharing, the methods in this approach either become ineffective [5] or impose high computation cost due to the use of optimization or search-based techniques [6], [7]. The second approach avoids the above issues by specifying a set of processors that are dedicated to resource access. However, this approach imposes additional migration overhead and is less favorable with frequent resource accesses [8]. In addition, as reviewed in Section II, most existing solutions are either tailored to a fixed scheduling method and a resource sharing protocol [9], or require specific schedulability analysis to conduct the search [6]. These limitations introduce applicability issues and even pessimism, making them even more challenging to apply in real-world systems.

This paper presents a universal task allocation method for FP-FPS (fully-partitioned fixed-priority scheduling) systems with spin locks, where shared resources are accessed by tasks from their host processors. Instead of the search-based or optimization methods that rely on specific analysis, the proposed allocation utilizes a resource contention model (RCM) that approximates the degree of resource contention between tasks. Based on this guidance, we allocate tasks following the principle of always allocating tasks with the highest resource contention to the same processor, to reduce resource competition, and hence, the blocking of tasks. Two implementations of the RCM are constructed given different levels of knowledge of the system. The first implementation produces approximations based on the resource usage of the application tasks with no knowledge of the underlying system. With more details of the system obtained, the second implementation improves the approximation accuracy by taking the major characteristics of spin locks into account, which further enhances the effectiveness of the proposed allocation method.

The advantages of the proposed method are multi-fold: (i) it can produce allocation solutions without detailed information of the underlying system; (ii) it can be universally applied in all FP-FPS systems with spin locks which is oblivious to the choice of priority assignments, resource sharing protocols and schedulability tests; and (iii) it can provide effective and efficient solutions by avoiding complicated search-based or optimization methods. The proposed method is particularly useful as a pilot solution during the initial design phase. In addition, it remains competitive with enhanced performance in later design phases with more detailed information about the underlying system obtained. The evaluation validates the feasibility of the proposed method and demonstrates that as a heuristic, it can outperform the state-of-the-art search-based methods by 13.6% on average (up to 24.2%) and significantly reduce the computation cost by 57x on average.

div.head: II. THE STATE-OF-THE-ART AND LIMITATIONS
div.p: The research on resource-aware task allocation forms a large body of work that covers a wide range of scheduling algorithms, resource sharing protocols, schedulability tests, etc [5]- [7], [9]- [14]. This section focuses on existing resource-aware allocation methods for FP-FPS and discusses their limitations.

Most existing methods execute critical sections on the host processors of tasks [5]- [7], [10], [11]. Following this approach, Lakshmanan et al. [5] proposed a synchronization-aware partitioning algorithm (SPA) that bundles all tasks that directly or transitively share the same resources and allocates task bundles to processors using the Best-Fit Decreasing heuristic. The SPA is generic which only utilizes the knowledge of resource usage. However, it suffers from the following limitation due to its task bundling and allocation techniques.

Limitation 1. The SPA [5] can result in heavy bundles that cannot fit into any processor, in which tasks are allocated without considering shared resources, and hence, cannot reduce contention [6], [9].

In order to achieve higher effectiveness, a portion of existing work addresses the allocation problem using optimization techniques [6], [15]. In [6], an optimization problem is formulated for resourceaware task allocation based on Integer Linear Programming (ILP). However, the ILP suffers from low scalability and is unfavorable in scenarios such as large-scale design space exploration [8]. In the same work, a search-based method named the Greedy Slacker (GS) is developed to find feasible both allocation and priority order of tasks using Audesly's Optimal Priority Assignment (OPA) and a schedulability test [16]. However, the search-based techniques (e.g., GS with OPA adopted) can only be applied with the original analysis for spin locks [17], which has a high degree of pessimism, despite the fact that more accurate analysis is available, e.g., the holistic analysis in [3], [8]. This leads to the following limitation.
Limitation 2. The search-based approach in [6] mandates the use of the original schedulability analysis, which lacks generality and introduces pessimism that undermines its performance [17].

Instead of mapping tasks to processors, Hsiu et al. [11] propose a method that allocates resources to processors and migrates a task to a specified processor each time when it requests a shared resource. This localizes the shared resources and can reduce resource contention between processors. As reported, the method [11] reduces the number of processors needed for scheduling a system. Following the same approach, a resource-oriented partitioning (ROP) method is constructed in [9], [12] to find a feasible number of dedicated processors for shared resources and task allocations using a search-based method with a specialized schedulability test. Two versions of ROP are provided which apply the priority ceiling protocol and the nonpreemptive protocol to manage resource accesses on the dedicated processors. It has been shown in [12] that the ROP outperforms a set of existing methods, including the GS in [6]. However, tasks under ROP can incur an additional migration overhead each time when they access a shared resource, i.e., migrate to and back from a dedicated processor. This can impose a non-trivial runtime overhead and leads to the following limitation [8], [18]. Limitation 3. With intensive resource access, ROP [9] can cause frequent task migrations which impose a non-trivial overhead, and thus, undermines the performance of the method [8].

In addition, most existing methods are tailored for a specific scheduling method and a resource sharing protocol [7], [10], or require a high computation cost due to the search-based techniques that require iterative computations on the worst-case response time of tasks for each allocation decision [6], [12]. These limitations make them challenging to apply in real-world industrial systems, in which full details of the underlying system might not be available in early design phases and large-scale design space exploration might be required. To address this, we propose a resource-aware allocation method that can offer effective and efficient solutions without detailed knowledge of the underlying system.

div.head: III. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: We focus on systems that contain a set of identical processors Λ and a set of sporadic tasks Γ scheduled under the FP-FPS scheme. The x th processor in Λ is denoted as λx. A task τi (the i th task in Γ) is defined by τi = {Ci, Ti, Di, Pi, Ai}, in which Ci is the pure worst-case execution time without accessing shared resources, Ti is the period, Di is the constrained deadline with Di ≤ Ti, Pi is the priority, and Ai is the allocation. Each task has a unique priority and a higher value of Pi indicates a higher priority. Function Γ(λx) returns the set of all tasks that are allocated to λx. For simplicity, we use U to denote the utilization of a given task or a task group, e.g., Uτ i and U Γ(λx) , respectively. Function |•| denotes the size of a given set, e.g., |Λ| gives the number of processors in the system.

The system also contains a set of shared resources R protected by spin locks. For a resource r k (k th resource in R), c k denotes the worstcase computation time on r k and N k i gives the number of requests to r k issued by τi in one release. Function F (•) denotes resources that are requested by given tasks. Resources that are shared among tasks in multiple processors are terms as global resources while ones that are accessed within a processor are called local resources. In addition, a spin-based resource sharing protocol is assumed for managing the shared resources, which covers a wide range of choices [3]. However, no assumption is made that specifies the protocol and the associated schedulability analysis for the system. We assume that a task can only hold one resource at any time. However, nested resource access can be trivially supported using group locks as discussed in [8].

div.head: IV. A UNIVERSAL RESOURCE-AWARE TASK ALLOCATION
div.p: This section presents a universal resource-aware task allocation method for FP-FPS with spin locks applied, in which shared resources are accessed by tasks directly on their host processors. Different from existing methods, the proposed method utilizes a resource contention model (RCM) that can approximate the degree of resource contention between tasks, termed the contention factor (CF). Using the approximated CF as guidance, the method produces allocation decisions following the fundamental principle that always (i) group tasks with the highest CF approximation and (ii) allocate task groups with the highest approximated CF to one processor.

As the RCM does not aim to compute a safe bound on the worst-case response or blocking time, it can produce quick CF approximations with a sufficient level of accuracy without detailed knowledge of the underlying system. This provides the key to the generality of the proposed allocation method which is universally applicable in all FP-FPS systems. In this section, we focus on the proposed allocation method assuming the presence of the RCM. In Section V, two implementations of the RCM are presented to demonstrate that the CF approximations can be effectively obtained with different levels of knowledge of the underlying system.

div.head: A. Overall Mechanism and Preliminaries
div.p: For a given set of tasks, the proposed allocation method forms a set of task groups G in which each group contains tasks with high resource contention. The notation Ga denotes a task group with an index a. In addition, a utilization bound U is applied for all task groups to bound the maximum utilization allowed for one group, i.e., U ≥ UG a , ∀Ga ∈ G. In this work, U is set to the average utilization of the system in each processor, i.e., U = UΓ/|Λ|. With G constructed, the allocation is then performed that assigns a task group to a processor based on the CF approximation between the group and existing tasks on that processor.

As described, both the group formation and allocation decisions in the proposed method are made based on the CF approximations provided by the RCM. To guide the allocation decision, the RCM is required to produce the CF approximation for any two given task groups, denoted as ∆(Ga, G b ). A higher value of ∆(Ga, G b ) indicates a higher degree of resource contention between the task groups. For Ga and G b that do not share any resources, the RCM will inform the allocator with ∆(Ga, G b ) = 0. In addition, an input with a single task τi is treated as a group with one task, i.e., {τi}. A detailed description of the computations of ∆(Ga, G b ) that are compliant with the above requirements is provided in Section V.

div.head: B. Task Grouping based on Resource Contention
div.p: The proposed task grouping technique follows the principle of always merging two groups that have the highest CF approximation with U enforced. By doing so, only the tasks with a high resource contention will be merged into one group, even if they share certain resources with other tasks in the system. In addition, the use of U effectively avoids the creation of heavy groups that cannot be fitted into any processor. This highlights the key difference with the SPA, which tends to form large task bundles due to Limitation 1 discussed in Section II.
Algorithm 1: Task group formation
div.formula: 1 G = ∅; 2 for each τ i ∈ Γ do 3 Ga = {τ i }; G = G ∪ Ga; 4 end 5 compute ∆(Ga, G b ), ∀Ga, G b ∈ G ∧ a ̸ = b; 6 while true do 7 (Ga, G b ) = argmax a,b {∆(Ga, G b ) | U Ga + U G b ≤ U }; 8 if ∆(Ga, G b ) = 0 ∨ (Ga, G b ) = ∅ then 9 return G; 10 end 11 Ga = Ga ∪ G b ; G = G \ G b ; 12 Compute ∆(Ga, Gs), ∀Gs ∈ G ∧ a ̸ = s; 13 end 14 return G;
div.p: Algorithm 1 presents the complete task grouping process based on the RCM. The algorithm takes all tasks in the system Γ as the input and initializes |Γ| task groups where each group contains a single task (lines 1-4). For any two groups Ga and G b , the CF approximation is computed using the RCM, i.e., the ∆(Ga, G b ) in line 5. Then, the group formation starts by identifying the pair of groups with the highest CF approximation, among any two groups that can satisfy UG a + UG b ≤ U (line 7). If such a group pair is obtained with a positive CF approximation, a new group is created by merging the two groups (line 11). In addition, the CF approximation between the newly-created group and the existing ones in G is computed for further group formation in the following iterations (line 12). This process finishes until each group is independent from others (i.e., ∆(Ga, G b ) = 0) or no groups can be merged with U enforced (lines 8-10). Due to the former condition, groups with a single task that does not share any resources will not be merged during the entire process. Example 1 illustrates the group formation process using four tasks and Characteristic 1 summarizes the key that addresses Limitation 1 discussed in Section II. Example 1. For a task set {τ1, ..., τ4}, they are initialized as a set of groups {G1 = {τ1}, ..., G4 = {τ4}}, in which each group contains one task. Assuming ∆(G1, G4) is the highest among all groups, they will be merged together if U is satisfied, i.e., {G1 = {τ1, τ4}, ..., G3 = {τ3}}. Then, if ∆(G2, G3) is the highest, G2 and G3 are merged even if they also have a positive CF approximation with G1, i.e., {G1 = {τ1, τ4}, G2 = {τ2, τ3}}. However, under SPA all tasks are grouped together regardless of the resource contention.

Characteristic 1. The proposed method forms a set of task groups in which tasks in each group has the highest contention. In addition, U is applied to avoid forming large task groups that cannot be allocated in a single processor. This addresses Limitation 1.
Algorithm 2: Resource-aware task allocation
div.formula: 1 for each Ga ∈ G do 2 Ωa = τ i ∈Ga ∆({τ i }, Ga\τ i ); 3 end 4 for each x ∈ [1... min{|G|, |Λ|}] do 5 Ga = argmax a {Ωa | ∀Ga ∈ G}; 6 A i = λx, ∀τ i ∈ Ga; G = G \ Ga; 7 end 8 while G ̸ = ∅ do 9 λx = argmin x {U Γ(λx) | ∀λx ∈ Λ}; 10 Ga = argmax a {∆(Ga, Γ(λx)) | ∀Ga ∈ G}; 11 if U λx + U Ga ≤ 1 then 12 A i = λx, ∀τ i ∈ Ga; G = G \ Ga; 13 else 14 for each τ i ∈ Ga, highest ∆({τ i }, Γ(λx)) first do 15 if U λx + Uτ i ≤ 1 then 16 A i = λx; Ga = Ga \ τ i ;

div.head: C. Allocation of Task Groups on Processors
div.p: With G constructed, Algorithm 2 is performed that maps G to a set of processors Λ. The algorithm starts by computing a weight Ωa for each Ga based on the CF (lines 1-3). This factor reflects the degree of the internal resource contention between tasks in Ga. The allocation is then performed in two steps. The first step produces an initial allocation for up to |Λ| groups in G based on Ωa (lines 4-7). Then, the second step decides the allocations of the rest of the task groups based on the guidance of the RCM (lines 8-23).

In the first step, the method identifies at most min{|G|, |Λ|} task groups with the highest Ωa and allocates each of these groups to one processor (lines 5-6). For groups that have the same Ωa, the one with a higher utilization is taken. This is feasible as all groups are formed with U enforced and U ≤ 1. By localizing tasks in these groups, we mitigate the contention between the tasks with the highest CF approximations in the system.

Following the initial allocation, the second step maps the unallocated groups following the rule of the λx with the least U Γ(λx) first and the Ga with the highest ∆(Ga, Γ(λx)) first (lines 9-10). This increases the chance of fitting a complete task group and can reduce resource contention in a general case. If Ga can be fitted into λx, all tasks in the group are assigned to this processor (lines [11][12]. Otherwise, to increase the success ratio of the allocation method with reduced contention, tasks in Ga are allocated individually, in which the one with the highest ∆({τi}, Γ(λx)) is always assigned to λx. However, under this case, if no task in Ga can be assigned to λx (i.e., the processor with the lowest utilization), the algorithm returns immediately with no feasible allocation being found (lines 19-21). The complete process finishes until every task is assigned with an allocation, i.e., Ai, ∀τi ∈ Γ. With the above descriptions, we conclude the following two characteristics of the proposed method.

Characteristic 2. The proposed method allocates tasks to processors based on the RCM without the need for a specific schedulability test, and hence, addresses Limitation 2. Characteristic 3. Tasks under the proposed method do not require additional runtime facilities, e.g., migrations in [12], and have negligible runtime overhead that is equivalent to the traditional FP-FPS system. This addresses Limitation 3.

This concludes the description of the proposed task allocation method. The time complexity of the proposed method is O(n 2 ), as at most ||Γ|×|Γ|| iterations are required to (i) compute ∆(Ga, G b ) for all group pairs in G, (ii) form task groups, and (iii) allocate the task groups to processors. As illustrated by the allocation process, the CF approximations provided by the RCM are vital to the proposed allocation. In the next section, we demonstrate that the CF approximations can be effectively obtained given different levels of knowledge of the underlying systems.

div.head: V. REALIZING THE RESOURCE CONTENTION MODEL
div.p: This section realizes the RCM required by the proposed task allocation method. Two implementations of the RCM are constructed with an increasing level of knowledge of the system. The first implementation approximates CF only based on the resource usage of tasks. The second improves the approximation accuracy by taking the major characteristics of spin locks into account, which further enhances the performance of the allocation method as shown in Section VI. We note that the RCM provides neither safe timing bounds for tasks with shared resources nor exactly accurate quantification of the resource contention between tasks. Instead, the RCM aims to produce CF approximations with a sufficient level of accuracy between tasks so that effective guidance can be provided for task allocation to reduce contention. By doing so, the RCM (and the allocation) can produce quick approximations and is decoupled from priority assignment algorithms, resource sharing protocols, and schedulability tests.

div.head: A. Universal Contention Factor
div.p: With no information about the underlying system (e.g., in the initial design phase), the CF can be approximated based on the resource usage of tasks with the intuition of more intensive resource access in general leads to a higher contention. Equation 1 computes the resource access intensity of a task group Ga to a resource r k , denoted as α(r k , Ga). This equation considers two major factors that can affect the degree of contention: (i) the resource access frequency of tasks in Ga to r k and (ii) the length of r k (i.e., c k ), in which an increase in either factor can cause a higher blocking on tasks competing for r k .
div.formula: α(r k , Ga) = τ i ∈Ga N k i Ti × c k(1)
div.p: Based on α(r k , Ga), the CF approximation (i.e., ∆(Ga, G b )) required by the allocation is computed in Equation 2. This equation first identifies the resources shared among both groups, i.e., r k ∈ F (τi) ∩ F (τj). Then, for each r k , the average value of the resource access intensity of the two groups is computed, which indicates the degree of contention on r k between the groups. Accordingly, a higher average intensity on r k reflects a higher contention on the resource of tasks between the groups in a general case. Finally, the CF is approximated as the sum of the average resource access intensity of all resources shared between Ga and G b .
div.formula: ∆(Ga, G b ) = r k ∈F (Ga)∩F (G b ) avg α(r k , Ga), α(r k , G b )(2)
div.p: With Equation 2, although Ga and G b share certain resources, the RCM will produce a low CF if the groups have a resource access intensity, indicating that they are less favorable to be allocated to the same processor. Similar to SPA, this RCM is universal which only utilizes the resource usage of tasks without any knowledge of the underlying system, e.g., the resource sharing protocol. However, the RCM guides the allocation with the resource contention into account, and hence, can lead to improved effectiveness.

div.head: B. Contention Factor for FIFO and Priority-based Spin Locks
div.p: As described in [3], spin locks can be broadly classified as unordered, FIFO and priority-based based on the order of service for resource requests. Among them, both the FIFO and priority-based spin locks impose a specific resource-accessing order, which can be captured by the RCM to provide more accurate CF approximations. This section constructs a finer-grained RCM by taking the resourceaccessing order as a priori knowledge.

Under FIFO spin locks, each global resource is associated with a FIFO queue that contains requests from all processors based on their arriving order, in which the task at the head of the queue is always granted with the resource [18]. This leads to Lemma 1.
Lemma 1. With FIFO spin locks, a request of τi to r k can be blocked at most once by requests to r k from a remote processor.

Proof. For non-preemptive spin locks, the resource access strictly follows the "pigeon-hole principle" in which at most one request can be issued from a processor at any time instance. This is proved in [3], [8]. As for preemptive ones, higher-priority tasks can preempt a spinning task τi for r k , however, these tasks cannot request r k after preempting τi. Otherwise, deadlocks can occur in which τi cannot be served as it is preempted by a task that is waiting (spinning) behind τi in the FIFO queue. Thus, a processor contains at most one request to a global resource at any time instant with FIFO spin locks.

Following Lemma 1, the contention that τi can incur from Ga under FIFO spin locks is estimated in Equation 3, denoted as ϕ f if o (τi, Ga). Notation N k i (t) gives the number of requests from τi to r k in a time duration t, i.e., N k i (t) = t T i × N k i . Assuming τi and Ga are allocated on two different processors, τi can incur at most N k i (Ti) blocking for accessing r k from the tasks in Ga.
div.formula: ϕ f if o (τi, Ga) = r k ∈R min N k i (Ti), τ j ∈Ga N k j (Ti) × c k(3)
div.p: As for the priority-based spin locks, we assume the priority of requests from τi to r k is known a prior, denoted as P k i . With prioritybased spin locks, tasks that request a global resource are ordered by their accessing priority and the one with the highest priority is always granted the resource. In this case, τi can incur blocking for accessing r k by all the high-priority requests to r k and at most one low-priority request from a remote processor [3]. A formal proof can be found in [3], [19]. Accordingly, the contention that τi can incur from Ga is approximated by Equation 4, assuming they are allocated to two different processors. We note that an additional request is added to reflect a potential blocking from a low-priority resource request.
div.formula: ϕ prio (τi, Ga) = r k ∈F (τ i )∩F (Ga) Ä τ j ∈Ga∧P k i
div.p: ) With Equations 3 and 4, the CF approximation between Ga and G b under both types of spin locks is obtained, as shown in Equation 5. This equation computes the sum of contention that tasks in both groups can incur if they are allocated to different processors, in which a higher value implies higher benefits for allocating both groups to the same processor (if possible).
div.formula: ∆(Ga, G b ) = τ i ∈Ga ϕ(τi, G b ) + τ j ∈G b ϕ(τj, Ga)(5)
div.p: We note that the transitive blocking from local high-priority tasks is not explicitly considered in the RCM. However, by guiding the allocation to map task groups with a higher ∆(Ga, G b ) to the same processor, it implicitly mitigates such blocking in a general case due to the reduced contention. In addition, this avoids over-complicated computations which might require additional information about the underlying system. In section VI, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the RCM and the allocation using a common-seen system setup.

div.head: VI. EVALUATION
div.p: This section evaluates the performance of the proposed resourceaware task allocation method against the state-of-the-art methods in terms of both effectiveness and efficiency. The following competing methods are considered: (i) a combination of Worst-Fit, Best-Fit, First-Fit, and Next-Fit heuristics as the baseline [6] (denoted as Any-Fit); (ii) the SPA in [5]; (iii) the ROP with the non-preemptive protocol applied [9]; (iv) the GS in [6]; and (v) the proposed Resource-aware task Allocation with the universal RCM (denoted as RAU) and the RCM for FIFO spin locks (denoted as RAF).

Experimental Setup: The evaluation applies a similar experimental setup used in [3], [8]. A system contains m ∈ [4,32] processors and n × m tasks with n = [1,9], where n gives the average number of tasks per processor. The utilization of tasks is computed using the UUniFast-Discard algorithm [20] given a total utilization of 0.1 × n × m. Task periods Ti are randomly generated from the range [1ms, 1000ms] in a log-uniform distribution with Di = Ti. The Deadline Monotonic Priority Ordering is applied to generate task priorities. The total computation time (including the time executing with shared resources) is then obtained, denoted as Ci = Uτ i × Ti.

The system contains m shared resources, and each resource has a length randomly decided in a given range L. A resource sharing factor κ = 0.3 is applied to define the percentage of tasks in the system that will request shared resources, in which each of such tasks can randomly request [1, m] resources. The maximum number of accesses from a task to a resource is given by N = [1,40]. Let C R i denote the total resource computation time of τi, we enforce that Ci -C R i ≥ 0 with Ci = Ci -C R i . For each system configuration, 1000 systems are generated and tested by each competing method.

Unless specified in the allocation method (e.g., ROP), the MSRP is applied to manage the shared resources in the system, which is a FIFO spin-based protocol that is common-seen in multiprocessor real-time systems [6], [9], [17]. For Any-Fit, SPA, RAU and RAF, the holistic schedulability analysis for MSRP is applied to evaluate system schedulability [3], [8]. However, the original MSRP analysis is applied in GS due to Limitation 2 described in Section II. In addition, a cost of 8.35µs for each migration triggered by ROP is added in its schedulability test. This overhead is measured and reported by [8] under the Linux operating system.

Observations: Figure 1 presents the system schedulability of the competing methods with a varied n. From the figure, we can observe that the proposed RAU constantly outperforms SPA, where both methods are performed based on the resource usage of the system. This validates the effectiveness of the proposed allocation and the universal RCM. In addition, both the RAU and RAF maintain an advantage over all other methods with n = [1,6]. Specifically, the RAF outperforms the GS by 12.8% and ROP by 19.5% with n = 5, respectively. The reason for this observation is that both GS and ROP have a certain degree of pessimism that undermines their effectiveness (Limitations 2 and 3 in Section II). In contrast, the proposed alloca- 2 and3 with an increased N and m respectively, where RAU dominates SPA while RAF outperforms all competing methods in most cases. For instance, RAF outperforms GS by 13.6% on average with a varied N and can schedule up to 24.2% more systems than GS in both figures. It is worth noting that with an increased N , the schedulability of ROP drops quickly. This is because the intensive resource accesses cause both high migration overhead and interference as all requests to a resource are accessed on a dedicated processor. In addition, the proposed methods constantly outperform SPA and ROP with an increased L, as shown in Figure 4. For example, the RAF outperforms ROP by 91.6% with L = [1µs, 75µs]. This is because the increase in the resource length causes a higher interference on a task when accessing r k by other requests on the same processor. This observation is consistent with that in [9]. However, with a high m or L, GS demonstrates strong schedulability due to its search-based approach that optimizes both task allocation and priority order.

Finally, we report the computation cost of the competing methods on an Intel i5-4460 processor with a CPU frequency of 3.20GHz. Table I presents the average (avg.) and standard deviation (std.) of the computation cost of the evaluated methods with varied n and m. As shown in the table, the SPA has the lowest computation cost due to its simplicity. As for the RAF, it requires much less computation time compared to both ROP and GS. Specifically, the computation cost of ROP and GS is about 4.9x and 57x higher than RAF on average for all settings shown in the table. In particular, although with a high schedulability, the GS demonstrates a 55x higher computation cost on average than the RAP with n = 8. However, in most cases, the RAP achieves a higher schedulability than all other methods with a much less computation cost. The reason is both GS and ROP use a searching method that requires iterative computations to bound the worst-case response time of tasks for each allocation choice, resulting in a much higher cost to find a feasible allocation solution.

In summary, the proposed allocation can outperform the state-ofthe-art methods in schedulability with a much less computation cost. The results validate that the constructed RCM can provide effective guidance without details of the underlying system, and verify the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed allocation method.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION
div.p: This paper presents a universal resource-aware task allocation method for FP-FPS with spin locks. The proposed method groups tasks contending for shared resources and allocates task groups on processors using the guidance of a resource contention model (RCM), which approximates the resource contention between tasks. Two implementations of the RCM are constructed with different levels of knowledge of the system, one being universal and another being more accurate. The evaluation demonstrates both the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed method over the state-of-the-art methods.
